appraisal_events.evidence: « C'est une grande famille que les Guermantes! »... « c'est à la Duchesse qu'est le château de Guermantes. Et c'est elle dans le pays qu'est madame la mairesse. C'est quelque chose. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Françoise repeatedly stresses the family's grandeur, wealth, château, and quasi-official local eminence, even treating the title 'mairesse' as beneath their true standing; the narrator's comic aside about her muddled reasoning ironizes her logic without denying the underlying claim of grandeur.

appraisal_events.evidence: « c'est un vrai seigneur, un grand pédant, on dirait qu'on lui a coupé la langue... Il ne vous fait même pas réponse quand on lui cause »... « On dit aussi qu'il est voleur comme une pie »... « c'est un vrai feignant que cet Antoine, et son «Antoinesse» ne vaut pas mieux que lui »
appraisal_events.explanation: Françoise portrays Antoine as haughty, silent toward her, idle, and reputedly dishonest, but the narrator flags her disclaiming remark as spoken 'sans sincérité,' framing her account as gossip rather than fully reliable judgment.

status_effects.explanation: Françoise's admiring account of the family's château and local eminence locally elevates the duchesse's standing, though the comic frame around Françoise's reasoning tempers full narrator endorsement.
Antoine is depicted as proud, idle, dismissive of Françoise, and rumored dishonest, clearly lowering his local standing, tempered slightly by the narrator's note undercutting Françoise's sincerity.

ambiguities: The narrator's comic comparison of Françoise's reasoning to Pascal ironizes her method of arguing for the Guermantes' grandeur without directly denying the substance of the claim, so the elevation is read as reported rather than fully narrator-endorsed.

The narrator's remark that Françoise speaks 'sans sincérité' undercuts the reliability of her blame of Antoine, though the specific charges of idleness and haughty silence are not themselves contradicted.
